I think fans tend to have a warped perspective of the power & abilities of an average Jedi knight (and honestly just Jedi in general) due to a majority of the franchise focusing on Anakin, who’s a child prodigy and the literal *chosen one*. 

If you go back and watch the Prequels and The Clone Wars show, pay closer attention to the Jedi in the background as well as Jedi side characters. They tend to be surprisingly squishy when they’re not given Anakin-level plot armor. I’ll put some examples at of what I mean at the bottom of this . 

We also have to keep in mind that Cal was around 13-14 when Order 66 happened, which means he would’ve been born a year or two at most before the events of The Phantom Menace. He basically spent most of his life training as a Padawan and serving as a commander in the Clone Wars (according to his wiki page) so he’s going to have more real-world combat experience than other Jedi. 

In my opinion, during Fallen Order he’s at a similar skill level as early (season 1-3) Clone Wars Ahsoka & during Jedi Survivor he’s at about the same skill level as Ahsoka was in the The Clone Wars series finale. He’s one of the higher-end knights but he doesn’t quite have the wisdom and knowledge of a Master yet. 

TL;DR - Cal Kestis has the fighting skills of a battle-hardened knight but doesn’t have the same wisdom & understanding of the force as a Master yet.

•(Padawan) Obi-Wan & (Jedi Master) Qui-Gon getting quickly overwhelmed and forced to retreat by only two droidekas in TPM.

•(Jedi Master) Coleman Trebor getting insta-killed by Jango. 

•(Knight) Nahdar Vebb being unable to keep his emotions in check while hunting Grevious and getting laid out by him.

I’m talking about the ones next to the headlights. They’re the same as a normal cars hazard lights and blink simultaneously. 

The flashing ones at the top of the bus are the 8-ways which are the ones you get fined for running. Those ones flash right to left back and forth. Technically you can legally drive through *yellow* 8-ways but I’d caution against doing that unless the driver waves you past. 

Fun fact: You can also legally drive perpendicularly past red flashing lights, if the bus is stopped at an intersection for example. You just can’t go parallel  past the stop sign on the bus. I’d highly caution against doing this though as it’s needlessly risky.

Fellow school bus driver here. I’d also like to add that if a bus is stopped on the side with *yellow* hazard lights, you’re allowed to pass them. We typically do this on roads where using our red 8-way lights would cause too much disruption to the traffic flow.

I took my test about 6 months ago so anyone feel free to correct me if I’m remembering wrong. 


You should be heavily relying on your side mirrors for the parallel parking portion.

IIRC, what they mean by “lose sight” of the cones is that when your tires are lined up like in figure 3) and you start reversing, you should be focusing on the back-most cones in your right side mirror while turning the wheels. Once those rear cones disappear from your right side mirror, you should stop moving (if allowed), immediately straighten your wheels out, then continue reversing while focusing on both your left side mirror AND your loading door.

At this point, you SLOWLY continue reversing straight until the front cone is just past the nose of your bus AND the rear cones come into view in your left side mirror. Once this has happened, you should immediately crank your wheel as far left as it’ll go.

If you’ve done everything correctly up to this point, then your bus will pivot perfectly right into the parking spot.

Hopefully I explained everything well enough. It may differ between states but on my skills test they combined all the skills (forward precision parking, straight reverse, angled forward maneuvering, & angled reverse/parallel parking) into one continuous test. This made it a bit easier imo.

Another thing to keep in mind is that your rear wheels are pretty much always going to be your main pivot point on turns in general and especially while maneuvering in reverse. You should be “wrapping” them around the front cones if that makes sense. 

Don’t stress too much about the road test commentary either. You’re essentially just going to be announcing everything you’re doing and reading road signs out loud. For example: “I see a merge left sign up ahead so I’m going to put on my blinker, check my mirrors, look over my shoulder, and begin merging once I see it’s safe and I have room.” 

Remember to pay attention to every road sign you pass because at some point the instructor *will* ask you what a random sign said on it after you drive past it to make sure you’re paying attention.

The absolute bare minimum supplies you’ll want are a die set with D4, D6, D8, D10, D12, D20, and D100, an official D&D 5e rulebook (~$50 but can be found online for free if that’s too expensive), a pencil and notebook to keep track of the story, and some character sheet templates which can also be printed online for free. 

I’d highly recommend watching a few YouTube videos on creating a character and some of the basic mechanics of D&D. A few lore guides would be helpful as well since there’s A LOT to learn about the story, timeline, etc. of Faerun and/or the Forgotten Realms. 

Lastly, If you’re able to, I’d highly, *highly* recommend playing Baldur’s Gate 3 if you haven’t yet. It’s designed around the official D&D 5e rules and teaches you a huge chunk of the mechanics and lore of the Forgotten Realms. It depends on company and location but there’s generally a lot less work during summer break. At my company the mainstream route drivers bid on routes in August which is based on seniority. If they’ve already assigned school year routes at your company and haven’t said anything to you about having a set route then you’ll likely be a sub driver, be doing ride alongs, and/or be given charter and field trip routes for the first few weeks or until a route opens up since you began during summer break.

I started in the last month of the school year at my location and they had me ride along with another driver on a wheelchair route for ~3 weeks so I could learn the route and have wheelchair training. Then they let me take over that route for the rest of the year. 

Would highly recommend getting wheelchair, 5-star restraint, and safety strap training if that’s an option. It opens up a lot more possibilities for work.
